pos: n. (the see in Flanders, archbishopric from 1559, held by Fenelon from 1695)
etymology: From the Gaulish Camaracum; the Dutch form is Kamerijk.
biblical_def: Cambrai on the Scheldt was a bishopric from the fourth century and from 1559 an archbishopric, its bishops ruling as temporal princes of the Empire over a wedge of territory between France and the Netherlands. The town gave its name to the League of Cambrai of 1508 and to the Ladies' Peace of 1529, and it was a notable centre of church music under Guillaume Dufay, who was a canon there. Its best-known archbishop was Francois Fenelon, appointed in 1695, author of the Telemaque and defender of Madame Guyon's quietism, who was condemned by Rome in 1699 and submitted at once from his own pulpit. The dictionary records Cambrai for Fenelon's submission, because it states the Roman principle exactly. He had written what he believed and he withdrew it on authority, not on argument. The Reformed order is the reverse: a text is answered from a text. “searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11) makes the hearer the examiner, “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21) makes the duty general, and “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) says what the examination is conducted with.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines quietism as the doctrine of the quietists, who placed religion in internal rest; submission as the act of yielding to authority; a recantation as the retraction of a declaration; authority as legal power; and a see as a bishop's seat.
webster_full: QUIETISM, n. Peace or tranquility of mind; apathy; the system of the Quietists, who maintained that religion consists in the internal rest or recollection of the mind.
SUBMISSION, n. The act of submitting; the act of yielding to power or authority; resignation.
RECANTATION, n. The act of recanting; a declaration that contradicts a former one.
AUTHORITY, n. Legal power, or a right to command or to act; power exercised by virtue of office.
SEE, n. The seat of episcopal power; a diocese; the jurisdiction of a bishop.

corruption_summary: See on the Scheldt, archbishopric from 1559, whose archbishop Fenelon submitted to Rome's condemnation of his book in 1699.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the order of appeal. Fenelon yielded to a verdict rather than to an argument, and Scripture puts the examination the other way round: “searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11), where the hearers judge the preacher by the text and not the text by the preacher.

The live temptation is to admire the humility and miss the mechanism. Submission to a tribunal that gives no reasons is not humility but abdication, and Paul assigns the testing to everyone, “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21). The instrument is named, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16), and the minister's qualification is a grip on it, “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9).

pos: n. (the hilltop see in Picardy whose school under Anselm produced the Glossa Ordinaria)
etymology: From Latin Laudunum; the modern French form has lost the medial consonants.
biblical_def: Laon stands on a long ridge above the plain of Picardy, a see from the sixth century and a royal city of the Carolingians. Its cathedral, begun about 1155, is one of the earliest great Gothic churches, with the famous carved oxen in its tower openings, set there in memory of the beasts that hauled the stone up the hill. Laon's greater importance is scholastic: Anselm of Laon, who taught there until his death in 1117, assembled with his pupils the Glossa Ordinaria, the standard marginal and interlinear commentary on the whole Bible, which became the basic working apparatus of every medieval theologian. Abelard studied under him and mocked him, with the ingratitude of the brilliant. The dictionary records Laon for the Gloss, which is the medieval church's most useful single achievement and also its most revealing. A Bible that arrives already surrounded by authoritative comment is a Bible under management. “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) is said of the text and not of the margin, and “searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11) assumes a reader permitted to reach the page.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a gloss as an explanatory comment; interlinear as inserted between lines; a margin as the edge of a page; commentary as exposition; and a scholastic as one versed in the schools.
webster_full: GLOSS, n. A comment; explanatory remark or note, intended to illustrate the subject; an interpretation.
INTERLINEAR, a. Written or inserted between lines before written or printed.
MARGIN, n. A border; edge; brink; verge; the edge of a page left blank or filled with notes.
COMMENTARY, n. A comment; exposition; explanation; illustration of difficult passages in an author.
SCHOLASTIC, a. Pertaining to a scholar, to a school or to schools; pertaining to the schoolmen.

corruption_summary: Picardy see whose school under Anselm of Laon compiled the Glossa Ordinaria, the standard medieval commentary on the whole Bible.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the distinction between the text and the apparatus around it. The Gloss was a magnificent tool, and the apostolic claim is made for the inspired words only: “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16). Comment may be useful; it is not breathed out by God.

The live temptation is to let an authoritative margin determine the page, which is what the Gloss came to do. Luke's commendation presumes direct access, “searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11), and the Psalmist's promise is attached to the words themselves, “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.” (Psa 119:130). Paul's own traditions are apostolic and no wider, “stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle” (2Th 2:15).

pos: n. (the Picardy see whose council of 1121 condemned Abelard and made him burn his own book)
etymology: From the Gaulish tribe the Suessiones, through Latin Suessiones; the final consonants are silent in French.
biblical_def: Soissons was the capital of the Roman Suessiones and the place where Clovis defeated Syagrius in 486 to begin the Frankish kingdom. It was a see from the third century and the site of several councils. Two concern the history of doctrine. In 1092 a synod at Soissons condemned Roscelin's account of the Trinity, and in 1121 another condemned Abelard's treatise on the Trinity and required him to throw the book into the fire with his own hands, which he did; he describes the humiliation in his Historia Calamitatum, and complains, with justice, that his judges had not read it. The dictionary records Soissons for that complaint. Abelard was often wrong and the procedure was worse: a book condemned unread and burned by its author is not a refutation. The Reformed method requires the opposite at every step. “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21) demands examination, “searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11) models it, and “speak thou the things which become sound doctrine” (Tit 2:1) asks for a positive statement rather than a bonfire.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a council as an assembly of ecclesiastics; a synod as an assembly of divines; heresy as a fundamental error in religion; to condemn as to pronounce guilty; and refutation as the act of proving false.
webster_full: COUNCIL, n. An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice.
SYNOD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.
HERESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
CONDEMN, v.t. To pronounce to be utterly wrong; to utter a sentence of disapprobation against.
REFUTATION, n. The act or process of refuting or disproving; the act of proving to be false or erroneous.

corruption_summary: Picardy see and council town, where in 1121 Abelard was made to burn his own treatise on the Trinity, condemned by judges who had not read it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that error is answered and not merely sentenced. Paul gives the church a method, “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21), and Luke commends a congregation for using it, “searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11). Neither describes a tribunal condemning an unread book.

The live temptation is to suppose that strong language against error excuses a careless process. Jude does command contention, “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3), and the contending is for a deposit that must first be understood. The positive charge Paul gives Titus is to “speak thou the things which become sound doctrine” (Tit 2:1), which is construction rather than combustion.

pos: n. (the Picardy cathedral town where John Calvin was born in 1509)
etymology: From Latin Noviomagus, the new market or field; the French form has contracted heavily.
biblical_def: Noyon in Picardy was a see from the sixth century, the place where Charlemagne was crowned king of the Franks in 768 and Hugh Capet king of France in 987, and the builder of one of the first great transitional Gothic cathedrals. Its importance to the Reformed churches is a birth: John Calvin was born at Noyon on 10 July 1509, son of Gerard Cauvin, a notary who served the cathedral chapter as its registrar and procurator. The connection was close enough that young Calvin held ecclesiastical benefices in the diocese from the age of twelve to fund his studies, and the family's later quarrel with the chapter over his father's accounts ended with Gerard dying excommunicate. The dictionary records Noyon as Calvin's birthplace and declines any shrine-making about it. He would have refused it himself; a man whose whole labour was to point away from men to a text is badly served by a plaque. “I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation” (Rom 1:16) is his subject, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) his instrument, and “it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21) his method.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a benefice as an ecclesiastical living; a chapter as a corporation of clergymen; a notary as a public officer who attests deeds; excommunication as expulsion from the communion of a church; and exposition as explanation.
webster_full: BENEFICE, n. An ecclesiastical living; a church endowed with a revenue for the performance of divine service.
CHAPTER, n. A corporation or community of ecclesiastics belonging to a cathedral or collegiate church.
NOTARY, n. An officer authorized to attest contracts or writings of any kind, to give them the evidence of authenticity.
EXCOMMUNICATION, n. The act of ejecting from a church; expulsion from the communion of a church.
EXPOSITION, n. A laying open; a setting to public view; explanation; interpretation.

corruption_summary: Picardy see and coronation town, birthplace of John Calvin on 10 July 1509, where his father served the cathedral chapter.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Calvin's own refusal of personal attention. His subject was never himself but a gospel he describes with Paul's words, “I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation” (Rom 1:16), and his instrument was a text he held to be “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) and nothing besides.

The live temptation runs in two directions, toward a cult of the man or toward treating him as a system. He was a preacher, and the thing he spent his life doing is named without dignity in Scripture: “it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21). The charge he obeyed through some two thousand sermons at Geneva is the plain “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2).

pos: n. (the Picardy see whose cathedral choir, the tallest ever built, collapsed in 1284)
etymology: From the Gaulish Bellovaci, the tribe, through Latin Bellovacum.
biblical_def: Beauvais in Picardy attempted the greatest building of the Gothic age and failed. The choir of its cathedral, begun in 1225, was raised to a vault some hundred and fifty-seven feet above the floor, the highest ever built, and in 1284 part of it fell. It was rebuilt with the bays subdivided and extra piers inserted, and the nave was never built at all; a tower added in the sixteenth century reached higher still and collapsed in 1573. The cathedral stands today as a choir and transept with no nave, among the most instructive buildings in Europe. Beauvais also supplied Pierre Cauchon, its bishop, who presided over the trial of Joan of Arc in 1431. The dictionary records Beauvais for the collapse, which preaches without assistance. “intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost” (Luk 14:28) is the Lord's own word about a tower and a builder who did not reckon, and “built his house upon a rock” (Mat 7:24) sets the whole business on its proper footing. A church may be ambitious; it may not be ambitious instead of being founded.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a vault as an arched roof; a buttress as a prop supporting a wall; to collapse as to fall together; presumption as groundless confidence; and a tower as a lofty building.
webster_full: VAULT, n. An arched roof, so constructed that the stones or other materials of which it is composed sustain and keep each other in their places.
BUTTRESS, n. A prop; a wall or abutment built archwise, serving to support another wall on the outside.
COLLAPSE, v.i. To fall together, as the two sides of a vessel; to close by falling together.
PRESUMPTION, n. Blind or headstrong confidence; unreasonable adventurousness; arrogance.
TOWER, n. A building raised to a considerable elevation above the adjacent ground or buildings.

corruption_summary: Picardy see whose cathedral choir, the tallest Gothic vault ever raised, partly collapsed in 1284; the nave was never built.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is reckoning before building. Christ tells a parable about exactly this, “intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost” (Luk 14:28), and the builder at Beauvais did not. The alternative He offers is not modesty but foundation: “built his house upon a rock” (Mat 7:24).

The live temptation is to read the ruin as an argument against ambition in church building, which is sentimentality. Scripture's question is about the base, “If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?” (Psa 11:3), and about the power relied on, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6). A low church on sand fails as surely as a high one.

pos: n. (the Burgundian archbishopric, seat of the earliest Gothic cathedral and of the council that condemned Abelard in 1141)
etymology: From the Gaulish tribe the Senones, through Latin Senones; the final consonant is not sounded.
biblical_def: Sens on the Yonne was an archbishopric whose province long included Paris, and its cathedral of St Etienne, begun about 1135, is generally reckoned the earliest Gothic cathedral of all, ahead of Saint-Denis in its structural ambition. Thomas Becket spent part of his exile at Sens and his vestments are kept in its treasury; William of Sens went on to rebuild the choir at Canterbury. The town is best known in doctrinal history for the Council of Sens in 1141, where Bernard of Clairvaux prosecuted Abelard, secured his condemnation before he could properly reply, and had the sentence confirmed at Rome. Abelard withdrew to Cluny and died within two years. The dictionary records Sens for that confrontation, and refuses to make a hero of either man. Bernard's doctrine of grace was better than Abelard's and his method was worse. Scripture gives the church both a duty and a manner: “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3) is commanded, and “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21) and “speak thou the things which become sound doctrine” (Tit 2:1) govern how.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a province as the circuit of an archbishop's jurisdiction; a metropolitan as an archbishop; an appeal as a removal of a cause to a higher court; dialectic as pertaining to reasoning; and contention as strife.
webster_full: PROVINCE, n. The district or division of a country subject to an archbishop or a bishop.
METROPOLITAN, n. The bishop of a mother church; an archbishop.
APPEAL, n. The removal of a cause or suit from an inferior to a superior tribunal.
DIALECTIC, a. Logical; argumental; pertaining to the art of reasoning.
CONTENTION, n. Strife; struggle; a violent effort to obtain something, or to resist a person, claim or injury.

corruption_summary: Burgundian archbishopric with the earliest Gothic cathedral, where the council of 1141 condemned Abelard at Bernard's prosecution.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that both the duty and the manner are commanded. Jude requires the fight, “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3), and Paul requires that it be conducted by examination, “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21). A prosecution that forecloses the reply satisfies the first and not the second.

The live temptation is to pick a side and absolve it. Bernard was nearer the truth about grace and Abelard was nearer the truth about procedure, and the dictionary says both. The positive charge stands over each of them: “speak thou the things which become sound doctrine” (Tit 2:1), and “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9), which is a grip on a word rather than on an advantage.

pos: n. (the Berry archbishopric of the Pragmatic Sanction of 1438, where Calvin studied law and Greek)
etymology: From the Gaulish Avaricum, later Bituriges, the tribal name; the modern form derives from the latter.
biblical_def: Bourges in Berry was an archbishopric whose cathedral of St Etienne carries one of the finest sets of thirteenth-century windows in France, and whose archbishop bore the title Primate of the Aquitaines. Two things give it a place here. The Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges, issued by Charles VII in 1438, asserted the liberties of the French church against papal appointment and taxation, and became the charter of Gallicanism for three centuries. And in 1529 or 1530 the young John Calvin came to Bourges to read law, and there learned Greek from Melchior Wolmar, a German Lutheran, in the years when his mind was turning. The dictionary records Bourges for the lectures rather than the cathedral. A man who intends to handle Scripture must be able to read it, and Wolmar's Greek is the unremarkable precondition of the Institutes. “Study to shew thyself approved unto God” (2Ti 2:15) is the command, “give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13) the charge, and “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) the reason either matters.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a primate as a chief ecclesiastic; a sanction as a ratification; Gallican is given under Gallic as pertaining to Gaul or France; Greek as the language of Greece; and diligence as steady application.
webster_full: PRIMATE, n. The chief ecclesiastic in the church; an archbishop who has jurisdiction over other bishops.
SANCTION, n. Ratification; an official act of a superior conferring validity on the act of some other person or body.
GALLIC, a. Pertaining to Gaul or France.
GREEK, n. A native of Greece; the language of Greece.
DILIGENCE, n. Steady application in business of any kind; constant effort to accomplish what is undertaken.
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
corruption_summary: Berry archbishopric of the 1438 Pragmatic Sanction, where Calvin read law and learned Greek from Melchior Wolmar about 1530.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that language study is not a luxury for a minister. Paul's command is “Study to shew thyself approved unto God” (2Ti 2:15) and his standing charge is “give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13), and a man who cannot read his text obeys neither well.

The live temptation is to treat learning as the enemy of piety, or piety as a substitute for learning. Neither is Reformed. The reason the grammar matters is the claim made for the words themselves, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16), and the model congregation is one that could check its preacher, “searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11).

pos: n. (the Limousin see of the abbey of St Martial, whose apostolic claim was a forgery)
etymology: From the Gaulish tribe the Lemovices, through Latin Lemovicum.
biblical_def: Limoges in the Limousin was a see and the home of the great abbey of St Martial, a centre of manuscript illumination and of early polyphonic music, and later of the enamel work that still bears the city's name. Martial himself was a third-century missionary bishop, but from the tenth century the abbey advanced a far larger claim: that he had been one of the seventy disciples sent out by Christ, personally commissioned, and the abbey produced a life and other documents to support it. The claim was pressed at a council at Limoges in 1031 and sustained for centuries before scholarship dismantled it. The dictionary records Limoges for the forgery, because it shows the pressure the medieval system put on history. A house with an apostolic founder outranked its neighbours and drew the pilgrims, so an apostolic founder was supplied. “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21) is the duty that would have stopped it, and “stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle” (2Th 2:15) limits what may be received to what came by apostolic word or letter.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a forgery as the crime of counterfeiting a writing; apostolic as pertaining to the apostles; enamel as a substance of the nature of glass; illumination as adornment with colours and gold; and tradition as that delivered orally.
webster_full: FORGERY, n. The crime of counterfeiting or falsifying a record, deed or other instrument in writing.
APOSTOLIC, a. Pertaining or relating to the apostles; according to the doctrines of the apostles.
ENAMEL, n. A substance of the nature of glass, differing from it by a greater degree of fusibility or opacity.
ILLUMINATE, v.t. To adorn with pictures or portraits, as a manuscript; to adorn with colors of various hues.
TRADITION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices, rites and customs from father to son, by oral communication.
scriptures: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle.
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:
corruption_summary: Limousin see whose abbey of St Martial forged documents from the tenth century claiming its founder was one of Christ's seventy disciples.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the limit on what may be received. Paul names his own traditions and bounds them, “stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle” (2Th 2:15), so that nothing outside apostolic word or letter carries the same weight. Limoges manufactured what it lacked, and the duty that would have caught it is “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” (1Th 5:21).

The live temptation is to treat such forgeries as medieval innocence rather than fraud. They were produced for advantage, and Paul's warning covers the species: “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men” (Col 2:8). The charge to a minister is custodial, “keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings” (1Ti 6:20), and a custodian who adds to the deposit has failed as surely as one who loses it.

pos: n. (the Anjou see and university town, home of the fourteenth-century Apocalypse tapestry)
etymology: From the Gaulish tribe the Andecavi, through Latin Andecavis; the city name is unrelated to the English word anger.
biblical_def: Angers on the Maine was the capital of Anjou, a see from the fourth century, and the seat of a university from 1337 that became one of the leading French law faculties. Its cathedral of St Maurice has twelfth-century glass and the earliest of the great Angevin vaults. Its extraordinary possession is a textile: the Apocalypse tapestry, woven between 1377 and 1382 for Louis I of Anjou to designs by Hennequin of Bruges and worked by Nicolas Bataille, originally some four hundred and sixty feet long and still surviving to about three hundred and thirty — the whole book of Revelation, scene by scene, in wool. The dictionary records Angers for that tapestry, which is the largest surviving attempt in any medium to set out a book of Scripture in order for people to look at. The ambition is admirable and the limit is the same as the carved cross's: an image can show the seals opened and cannot tell a man what they mean. “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17) names the appointed channel, and “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.” (Psa 119:130) the effect words have.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a tapestry as a woven hanging; the apocalypse as the book of Revelation; a seal as that which confirms; to weave as to unite threads; and revelation as the act of disclosing to others what was unknown.
webster_full: TAPESTRY, n. A kind of woven hangings of wool and silk, often enriched with gold and silver, representing figures of men, animals, landscapes, &c.
APOCALYPSE, n. Revelation; discovery; disclosure; the name of the last book of the Bible.
SEAL, n. A piece of metal or other hard substance, usually round or oval, on which is engraved some image or device.
WEAVE, v.t. To unite threads of any kind in such a manner as to form cloth.
REVELATION, n. The act of disclosing or discovering to others what was before unknown to them.
scriptures: So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
corruption_summary: Anjou see and university town, home of the Apocalypse tapestry woven 1377 to 1382, the largest surviving pictorial setting of a book of Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the credit and the limit of pictures. The Angers tapestry sets out Revelation in order on a scale no other medium has matched, and the aim is the Psalmist's, “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.” (Psa 119:130). The ambition deserves respect.

The live temptation is to make images do the work of words. Paul names the channel God appointed, “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17), and the instrument, “it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21), which is a man speaking. The complete pattern adds explanation to reading, as Nehemiah's Levites did when they “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.” (Neh 8:8).

pos: n. (the Breton see and city of the Edict of 1598 that gave the Huguenots legal toleration)
etymology: From the Gaulish tribe the Namnetes, through Latin Namnetum; the Breton form is Naoned.
biblical_def: Nantes at the mouth of the Loire was the chief city of Brittany and a see from the fourth century, but it enters Reformed history for one document. The Edict of Nantes, issued by Henry IV in April 1598, ended the Wars of Religion by granting the Huguenots liberty of conscience throughout France, public worship in specified places, full civil rights, their own courts within the parlements, and a number of fortified towns of security. It held, with erosion, for eighty-seven years, until Louis XIV revoked it by the Edict of Fontainebleau in October 1685, after which some two hundred thousand Protestants left France for England, the Netherlands, Prussia and the American colonies. The dictionary records Nantes for both dates. The Edict was not a theological concession but a political settlement, and it was enough; the Revocation taught the Reformed churches what a settlement is worth when the sovereign changes his mind. “ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free” (Joh 8:32) is Christ's account of what makes men free, and “here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14) is the right expectation of any charter.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an edict as a public ordinance; toleration as the allowance of religious opinions; revocation as the act of recalling; a refugee as one who flees for safety; and conscience as the moral faculty.
webster_full: EDICT, n. That which is uttered or proclaimed by authority as a rule of action; an order issued by a prince to his subjects.
TOLERATION, n. The act of tolerating; the allowance of that which is not wholly approved; allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state.
REVOCATION, n. The act of recalling or calling back; the act of annulling or making void.
REFUGEE, n. One who flies to a shelter or place of safety; one who, in times of persecution or political commotion, flees to a foreign country for safety.
CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; the faculty by which we judge of the moral rectitude of our own actions.

corruption_summary: Breton see and the city of the 1598 Edict granting the Huguenots toleration, revoked by Louis XIV in 1685 and followed by mass emigration.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is where liberty actually comes from. The Edict gave the Huguenots eighty-seven useful years and could be withdrawn by a signature. Christ grounds freedom elsewhere, “ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free” (Joh 8:32), and that grant has no revocation clause.

The live temptation is to make a legal settlement the measure of the church's security, which the Revocation of 1685 corrected brutally. Hebrews sets the expectation for every charter and city, “here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14). What remained to the refugees was the thing Paul refused to be ashamed of, “I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation” (Rom 1:16), and the duty Jude lays on them in exile, “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3).
